17 An object with a mass of 100 g falls a vertical distance of 10 m.
What is the change in the gravitational potential energy of the object?
A
1 J
B
10 J
C
100 J
D
10 000 J

hints: Notice the mass is given as $100 \text{ g}$ while the height is $10 \text{ m}$ - the energy formula needs mass in kg.
Connect the fall to gravitational potential energy change $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h$ with $g \approx 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Convert $100 \text{ g}$ to $0.10 \text{ kg}$ first, then multiply $m \times g \times \Delta h$ and check the result is in joules.
walkthrough: Identify the given data: $m = 100 \text{ g}$, vertical drop $\Delta h = 10 \text{ m}$, and $g \approx 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Convert mass to SI base units: $100 \text{ g} = 0.10 \text{ kg}$ because $1000 \text{ g} = 1 \text{ kg}$.
State the governing rule for change in gravitational potential energy: $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h$.
Substitute values with units: $\Delta E_p = 0.10 \text{ kg} \times 10 \text{ m s}^{-2} \times 10 \text{ m}$.
Calculate the intermediate product: $0.10 \times 10 = 1.0$, then $1.0 \times 10 = 10$, giving $10 \text{ J}$ with correct energy units.

A.explanation: Too small by a factor of 10, obtained if $g$ is taken as $1$ instead of about $10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.

B.explanation: Correct value from $mg\Delta h$ with mass in kg: $0.10 \times 10 \times 10 = 10 \text{ J}$.

C.explanation: Obtained by forgetting to convert 100 g to 0.10 kg and using $100 \times 10 \times 10$ without unit conversion.

D.explanation: Far too large, obtained by using mass as 100 and height as 10 with an extra factor of 10 error.
